planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil; Angustifolia keeps a looser, more open habit than common English boxwood and benefits from light annual shaping rather than hard shearing.

directions: Angustifolia is an old English boxwood selection distinguished by narrow, elongated leaves rather than the broad oval foliage of common boxwood, giving the shrub a finer, more willowy texture up close. It builds into a loose rounded mound over many years and takes well to light pruning that preserves its naturally airy outline instead of forcing it into a dense sheared ball. Part of a long-standing group of leaf-form English boxwood selections grown mainly by specialty collectors and historic gardens, it suits borders and mixed shrub plantings where a softer-textured boxwood is wanted alongside bolder-leaved companions.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil and stake young plants to establish a strong central leader before the arching, drooping branch habit develops.

directions: Pendula is a plain green weeping form of English boxwood, distinct from gold-variegated weeping selections, grown for its slender branches that arch outward and cascade at the tips as the plant matures. Young plants need staking to build height before the weeping character becomes pronounced, and little pruning beyond removing wayward shoots is needed once the form is established. It works best as a specimen or accent where its irregular, almost sculptural outline can be viewed from several angles rather than crowded into a mixed hedge line.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; its fine, small-scale leaves make it a good candidate for close-up edging rather than large-scale hedging.

directions: Myosotifolia takes its name from its tiny, narrow leaves, reminiscent in scale to those of forget-me-nots, which give the shrub an especially fine, dense texture compared with standard English boxwood. Growth is slow and compact, building into a tidy rounded form that needs only light trimming to keep its outline neat. It belongs to a long-grown group of small-leaved English boxwood selections valued by collectors for fine-textured edging, low formal borders, and detailed topiary work where larger-leaved cultivars would look coarse.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil with some direct sun to keep leaf size and color at their best.

directions: Latifolia shares the same large, leathery, rounded leaves found on the better-known variegated Latifolia Maculata, but stays plain dark green rather than developing gold mottling. It is a vigorous, large-growing English boxwood form that takes many years to reach full size and tolerates heavier pruning than fine-leaved selections, making it well suited to substantial hedges or large topiary shapes where bold leaf texture is an asset. Its broad foliage also reads well from a distance, which is useful in bigger landscape settings where smaller-leaved boxwood cultivars would disappear visually.

common_name: Columnaris Boxwood (Old Narrow Columnar English Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil and tip-prune lightly each year to keep growth tight and even along the narrow upright form.

directions: Columnaris is an old narrow, upright English boxwood selection that predates the modern columnar hybrids now common in the trade, holding a dense naturally vertical habit with little tendency to splay open with age. Growth is slow, so established plants require only occasional tip-pruning to maintain an even, uniform column rather than heavy annual shearing. It has long been used in formal gardens as a vertical accent or narrow screen in tight spaces where wider boxwood forms would quickly crowd a path or doorway.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; Pincushion naturally holds a tight dome shape and rarely needs shearing to look formal.

directions: Pincushion is a dwarf littleleaf boxwood selection that naturally forms a dense, evenly rounded mound resembling a sheared cushion without any clipping at all, a habit that sets it apart from boxwood cultivars that need regular shearing to stay tidy. Its small, closely packed leaves hold good color through the growing season and give the plant a fine, uniform texture at a modest mature size. It works well massed as a low, no-maintenance edge or border, or used singly as a soft rounded accent among perennials and other low shrubs.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars

common_name: Little Favorite Boxwood (Compact Dwarf Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; Little Favorite tolerates heat and humidity well and needs only light shearing to keep a tight, rounded outline.

directions: Little Favorite is a compact, slow-growing littleleaf boxwood selection long favored in southern landscapes as a lower-maintenance alternative to English boxwood in hot, humid climates. It builds a dense, evenly rounded form with small dark green leaves and holds its shape with only occasional light shearing rather than frequent heavy pruning. Its small mature size and reliable habit make it a dependable choice for low formal hedging, foundation plantings, and parterre-style edging where a tidy, predictable boxwood is needed.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Boxwood Cultivars
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil with some direct sun to keep the leaf margins bright.

directions: Elegans is an old dwarf English boxwood selection with small, narrow, pointed leaves finely edged in creamy white, giving the foliage a delicate, lace-like appearance distinct from the bolder variegation of Elegantissima. Growth is slow and naturally compact, so it needs very little pruning to hold a neat, dense form. Grown mainly by specialty and collector nurseries, it suits small-scale edging, rock gardens, or container specimens where its fine texture and subtle variegation can be appreciated at close range.

common_name: Herrenhausen Boxwood (Cold-Hardy German English Boxwood Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil sheltered from harsh winter wind and sun while young.

directions: Herrenhausen takes its name from the historic Herrenhausen Gardens in Hannover, Germany, and is grown by European nurseries as a dense, compact English boxwood form valued for reliable winter hardiness in continental climates. It forms a tidy rounded shrub with small dark green leaves and responds well to shearing for formal hedging or topiary. Where winters are colder than standard English boxwood comfortably tolerates, this selection offers a sturdier option without sacrificing the classic dense, fine-textured look.

common_name: Castle Point Boxwood (Dense Narrow Columnar Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil and tip-prune young plants lightly to encourage dense branching from the base upward.

directions: Castle Point is a dense, narrow, upright English boxwood form grown in the European nursery trade as a lower-maintenance alternative to clipped columnar hedging. It holds a tight vertical habit with good branching from the base, reducing the bare-legged look that can develop on some narrow upright shrubs over time. Left largely unsheared it still keeps a neat columnar silhouette, making it useful for narrow side-yard screens, formal gateway plantings, or repeated vertical accents along a walkway.
